pl-l3d36c2-d1e115.summary: Asks whether one possesses all virtues equally, or some more fervently and others less.

pl-l3d36c2-d1e118.summary: Reports that some think one may have some virtues more and others less, as patience stood out in Job, humility in David, meekness in Moses, and that one merits more by a virtue one has more fully. But none merits more than charity or is had more fully than charity, which begets the others; these are the 'many faces' of which Paul speaks.
claims: Some hold that virtues are possessed unequally.
No virtue is had more fully than charity or merits more.

pl-l3d36c2-d1e127.summary: States that others say more truly that all virtues exist together and equally in whoever has them, so that one equal to another in one virtue is equal in all.
claims: All virtues are together and equal in whoever has them.

pl-l3d36c2-d1e131.summary: Quotes Augustine: the virtues, though understood differently, are in no way separated, so that those equal in fortitude are equal also in prudence, justice, and temperance; if one excelled in prudence, the other's fortitude would be less prudent, and so they would not be equal in fortitude.
claims: Those equal in one virtue are equal in all.

pl-l3d36c2-d1e140.summary: Draws out that all virtues are not only connected but equal in the soul. When someone is said to excel in one virtue, as Abraham in faith and Job in patience, it refers to outward use or comparison with others, because he shows that habit most or performs its work especially.
claims: Excellence in a particular virtue refers to outward acts or comparison with others.

pl-l3d36c2-d1e146.summary: Quotes another passage where Augustine allows inequality: even if one who has one virtue has all, sins are not equal, since among the depraved some are worse. And if, as is more true, the soul's intentions are like members, some more illuminated by charity, some less, some not at all, then one can have one virtue and not another, or one more and another less. Virtue is charity, by which what is to be loved is loved; it is greater in some, lesser in others, absent in some, and full beyond increase in no one in this life.
claims: Virtue is charity, which is greater in some and lesser in others.
No one in this life has charity that cannot increase.

pl-l3d36c2-d1e158.summary: Interprets this: one can be said to have one virtue more than another because charity moves one more in the act of one virtue than of another; thus by difference of acts one has virtues more or less or not at all, while having them all together and equally as habit or essence. The married just man lacks continence in act though he has it in habit.
claims: Virtues are equal in habit but differ in act.
One may have a virtue in habit without its act.

pl-l3d36c2-d1e161.summary: Asks why, then, sins are not equal, and answers: perhaps because one who sins more gravely acts more against charity, one who sins lightly less. For no one (sentence continues).
claims: Sins are unequal according to how much they oppose charity.

pl-l3d36c2-d1e164.summary: Completes the answer: no one sins except by acting against charity, the fullness of the Law; so 'whoever offends in one point is guilty of all' means he acts against charity, on which all things hang.
claims: Offending in one point is guilty of all because it acts against charity.

pl-l3d36c2.summary: Asks whether one possesses all virtues equally. Some hold that one virtue may be had more than another, as patience in Job, humility in David, meekness in Moses, but none more than charity. Others more truly say the virtues are all together and equal in whoever has them; Augustine argues that equals in fortitude are equal in prudence too, else one's fortitude would be less prudent. Pre-eminence in one virtue, like Abraham in faith, refers to outward acts or comparison with others. Another passage of Augustine, denying that sins are equal, allows that virtue is charity, more in some, less in others, and that one may have one virtue more than another or lack one. Lombard reconciles: all virtues are had together and equally as habit or essence, but in act one more, another less, or not at all, as the married just man has continence in habit but not in act. Sins are unequal because some act more against charity, on which all depends.
claims: Some hold that virtues may be possessed unequally, but none more than charity.
Lombard holds, as more true, that all virtues are equal in whoever has them.
Pre-eminence in a virtue refers to outward acts or comparison with others.
Virtues are equal in habit but may differ in act.
Sins are unequal because some go more against charity.
